title: Epistemic modal logic
summary:
Epistemic modal logic is a subfield of modal logic that is concerned with reasoning about knowledge. While epistemology has a long philosophical tradition dating back to Ancient Greece, epistemic logic is a much more recent development with applications in many fields, including philosophy, theoretical computer science, artificial intelligence, economics, and linguistics.

The basic modal operator of epistemic logic, usually written K, can be read as "it is known that," "it is epistemically necessary that," or "it is inconsistent with what is known that not." Epistemic logic can be an example of multimodal logic applied for knowledge representation. Most attempts at modeling knowledge have been based on the possible worlds model, in which the set of possible worlds is divided between those that are compatible with an agent's knowledge and those that are not.

While philosophers since Aristotle have discussed modal logic, and Medieval philosophers such as Avicenna, Ockham, and Duns Scotus developed many of their observations, it was C. I. Lewis who created the first symbolic and systematic approach to the topic in 1912. It reached its modern form in 1963 with the work of Saul Kripke. The Finnish philosopher G. H. von Wright's 1951 paper An Essay in Modal Logic is seen as a founding document, but it was not until 1962 that Jaakko Hintikka wrote Knowledge and Belief, the first book-length work to suggest using modalities to capture the semantics of knowledge.

Epistemic logic has been combined with ideas from dynamic logic to create dynamic epistemic logic, which can be used to specify and reason about information change and exchange of information in multi-agent systems. The modal logic S5 (also known as KT45) is primarily used for epistemic reasoning, though it is debatable whether S4 describes epistemic logic better. The masked-man fallacy is a related concept in philosophical logic where one makes illicit use of Leibniz's law, failing to recognize that the law cannot account for intensional contexts.
